responseSet.title: Recent Research in Developmental Psychology
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Recent Research in Developmental Psychology

Mary Boston

Mary Boston

Mary Boston  

There has long been a gulf between academic psychology and psychoanalysis and nowhere has this been more marked than in the field of infant understanding, as evidenced by the variety of theories of child development which have emerged. A crucial point of divergence has been in relation to the kind of evidence which is offered in support of these theories. In trying to understand a young child's mental processes we are presented with enormous problems and possible sources of error. Bion has pointed out that there is not only the semantic gap to be bridged but also the question of the scientific propriety of attributing to infants experiences similar to our own. “Though the difficulties of penetrating the adult mind in analysis are great they are less so than attempting to penetrate the infant's by speculative hypothesis.” (Bion 1962).

On the whole, academic psychology has in the past coped with this problem by restricting investigation to those areas which have been considered suitable for scientific study, namely behavioural observations in controlled conditions, often with infants apart from their mothers and presented with a variety of standard objects. Areas of ‘speculative hypothesis’, such as the infant's feelings and emotional experience and relationships have often been left strictly alone, resulting in what Bryant (1974) has called “the psychologist's bleak picture of the young child's capabilities”. Indeed infants have been deemed unsuitable subjects for scientific investigation. Theories of child development have often seemed to psychoanalytic observers to give undue weight to cognitive factors or not to allow for the interrelationship of cognitive and emotional aspects of personality development.

Psychoanalytic interest in the study of child development began very early, in fact with Freud. To quote Hartmann (1950), “Analysis is also, and has always been, in Freud's work, general psychology. Freud's aim, expressed as early as in the Nineties, in material recently published, was to get insight into the entirety of mental functions and not only in the pathology of neuroses”. He (Freud) “complained that the direct observations of child psychologists are frequently questionable because they describe phenomena not really understood in their relationships and in their dynamic impact — while, on the other hand, the conclusions which we reach on the basis of analysis with adults have the disadvantage that we gain them through … reconstructions … and… many detours of thought.” Hartmann adds that while some part of this disadvantage was corrected by the development of child analysis, some of it yet remained. Indeed reconstructive theories of child development have usually been considered by psychologists to be unsupported by objective evidence and not capable of scientific evaluation or confirmation. Hartmann suggests however “the mutual checking of the data revealed by one method against those revealed by the other promises a more complete insight. Theories about early developmental stages have to be built on data of both reconstruction and direct observation.

responseSet.title: Psychotherapy of a Young in-Patient with Dystonia
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy of a Young in-Patient with Dystonia**

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur  

Individual psychotherapy in a hospital in-patient unit differs in some respects from work in Child Guidance or out-patient settings. In particular the staff and other patients in the Unit form a duplicate family background during the period of the child's stay. The therapist therefore is regarded as being more closely linked with this ‘family’ than is usually the case. Frequently the patient appears to feel as if the therapist represents one of the parents, and the Unit the other. His efforts to manipulate them against each other, or his capacity to feel that they are working harmoniously together, can be seen close at hand and clearly. Further it offers an opportunity of inter-relating individual psychotherapeutic work with the temporary home environment, which is specific to this type of setting.

A case is described here of a boy who was admitted to the Department of Psychological Medicine in a Children's Hospital. He was suffering from both somatic and psycho-neurotic disorders, and in this respect was somewhat characteristic of the in-patient population, as also in the fact that while his disability was severe, no definite diagnosis had been made.

Pierre, a pale red-headed boy, was the son of a professional couple. His frame was short and slight with a severe postural deformity, which included sitting and walking bent almost double. The movement of head and neck was strained and not well-controlled. In walking there was a tendency for the right foot to turn outwards at a sharp angle. In addition he had great difficulty in vocalising, so that he spoke little, in a struggling whisper, while breathing in (instead of on exhalation). This sometimes meant that he stuttered over words and was difficult to hear. The diagnosis of dystonia musculorum deformans was considered, and remains a possibility, but since despite extensive investigation no organic basis could be established, it was suggested that there might be some form of conversion hysteria or allied psychogenic element involved. On this basis, partly for observation, he was referred to the in-patient unit of the Hospital for Sick Children. At the time of admission he was about twelve and a half years old.

responseSet.title: A Five-Year Old Child and Her Grandmother -Therapeutic Encounters in General Practice
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Five-Year Old Child and Her Grandmother -Therapeutic Encounters in General Practice

Kenneth Sanders MD

Kenneth Sanders

Kenneth Sanders  

When there is an opportunity in general practice to bring psycho-analytic ways of understanding to bear on the puzzled distress of the man-in-the-street or the family in the waiting room, the impact is deeply felt on both sides.

The setting provides direct access to people who know nothing about psychotherapy, as well as to those who have sought referral to a clinic, and been rejected, or have grown weary of waiting, or have been offered an inadequate therapy.

Asked by a patient in general practice, a woman in her fifties, to provide a sedative for her five-year old grand-daughter, the only child of her daughter who had died a month ago, I found that she was mildly surprised at my suggestion that she present the child. She explained that Sally's mother had died after many months in hospital, of a wasting illness. Her father's grief had given him the appearance of coldness towards his daughter, he had scandalised the family by consulting his diary and finding a previous engagement that would prevent him from visiting her at his mother-in-law's house. So they were planning to adopt her, and their one-bedroomed flat would have to be exchanged for a larger one. In the meantime Sally seemed to have taken the loss well, did not refer to the matter, and the family were careful not to show grief in her presence.

There was just one difficulty, Sally was refusing to go to bed at night, and would not go to her new school.

I suggested that it was most likely that she was after all suffering from the effects of her loss, but grandmother reasoned against this, repeating that the mother had been ill for a long time, and away from home, that they were all careful to shield Sally, and besides the idea of death was not new to her, a favourite uncle on the father's side had died six months earlier.

Sally and her parents were unknown to me, but I knew the grandparents to be affectionate, unpretentious, homespun, saddened by this cruel death, not accustomed by culture to express more than the minimum of grief, subdued now, but determined to succour the little victim, yet floundering in their lack of psychological insight.

responseSet.title: A View of ‘King Lear’
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A View of ‘King Lear’

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller  

People have always accorded ‘King Lear’ a special place in the Shakespearian canon: they have never doubted its magnitude, the fact that in some way it overtops even Shakespeare's other tragedies, but they have felt on reflection some puzzlement, some reservation, as though something eluded them. Either they come to the conclusion that the fault must somehow somewhere lie in the play, as Dr. Johnson, Lamb or Coleridge did, or they decide that their own response is at fault, that they have skirmished at the edge instead of fighting to the centre. These feelings persist even in those who have experienced the power of the play to the full. This is a paradox which I think may be explained if we realise that audiences have intuitively felt just as Shakespeare intended them to feel, but that to a certain degree they have not been able to understand why they felt thus, nor perhaps exactly what they were feeling. I do not know of anyone who has come further in apprehension than Charles Lamb. He chooses to isolate his difficulty in the contention that the play is incapable of being acted on the stage — a contention which does not really accord with common experience — but at the same time he expounds brilliantly on the source of the play's power.

He writes:

“The greatness of Lear is not in corporal dimension, but in intellectual: the explosions of his passion are terrible as a volcano: they are storms turning up and disclosing to the bottom that sea, his mind, with all its vast riches. It is his mind which is laid bare.”

This is what the audience feels. The play is about the inner world of Lear. Other critics have added to our understanding by considering what the play has to say about the fight for redemption of an individual soul, the conflicts which arise in the family, the war in the body politic, the struggle between good and evil in all creation. These, and many other lines of enquiry, are to my mind profitable and illuminating. But I still think that Lamb gets to the centre when he says “We see not Lear, but we are Lear, — we are in his mind.” The play is to me a journey into the interior, a picture of man's internal world. Man is the microcosm on whose model all the macrocosms of family, state and world are formed. So a full understanding of the play depends upon a full understanding of what goes on in Lear's mind. We may be helped in our attempt to get this understanding by paying as close attention as possible to what Lear actually says, not even passing lightly over the fragmented lines of his madness (as I think is almost always in effect done), but trying to grasp everything both in the context of the whole play and of the whole character who voices Lear's thoughts.

responseSet.title: The Effect on a Child of a Mother Who Though Physically Present Was Emotionally Unavailable
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Effect on a Child of a Mother Who Though Physically Present Was Emotionally Unavailable**

Helen Carr and Jean Leared

Jean Leared

Jean Leared  

Introduction

This paper seeks to illustrate some of the consequences for a young child of a prolonged depression in his mother. It shows what may happen when a mother though physically present is emotionally absent, as David's mother was throughout much of the first year of his life, and highlights the dangers that beset such a child.

Some attempt is made to suggest the nature of the precipitating factor in Mrs. B.'s depression and to make links between her child's symptomatology as reported and observed, and her own depression. An account is also given of the therapeutic intervention, by a child psychotherapist and a psychiatric social worker, whereby the unsatisfactory cycle of relations which had been set in motion was ameliorated.

We are dependent for information about what took place in David's first two years upon reports from the health visitor and the Maternity and Child Welfare Clinic, from the parent's own account of it and from what could be gleaned from the treatment situation.

It is known that a mother who is depressed is in a withdrawn state and therefore less able than is usually the case to be sensitive and to respond appropriately to her infant's needs and that an infant faced with this situation will find his own particular way of reacting to it according to his make-up.

Fortunately, most mothers are not severely depressed for as long as David's mother was. However, Joyce Robertson (1965) from direct observation has reported the effect on two infants of the withdrawal of their mothers’ normally sensitive handling of them over a period lasting only two weeks, and the lasting effect of the damage to their relationships and development which the experience had and the different outcomes for the mothers and babies concerned.

Work with the Child Psychotherapist: Miss Helen Carr Referral

David was referred to the Clinic when two years and three months old by his general practitioner, who sent reports from the Maternity and Child Welfare Clinic and the health visitor.

responseSet.title: Babyhood by Penelope Leach Published by Penguin Books.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Babyhood by Penelope Leach Published by Penguin Books.

Ann Hurry

Ann Hurry

Ann Hurry  

This is an impressive book. It covers infant development from birth until two years of age and is aimed both at parents and at professionals working with parents or children. Dr. Leach tackles her vast subject by dividing infancy into five periods from ‘the first six weeks’ to ‘the second year’. It is thus possible to study development in any one period in detail: each section covers not only the fundamental patterns of feeding, sleeping, elimination, motility and perception, but also the growth of the sense of self via the integration of percepts, and the growth of relationships to objects. It is also possible, by studying the relevant chapters from each section, to follow the development of any particular function.

While the content is based upon a foundation of considerable scholarship, the style is clear and straightforward. Dr. Leach never dictates. She does not tell parents what to do, but rather sets out what is known about the infant and about the effects of different forms of handling, and leaves the choice to the parents. In setting out the known facts she makes use of research findings from many related fields, often succintly summarising relevant work, so that the book also provides a valuable compendium of research findings. Some findings, based upon her own studies, are published here for the first time.

It is evident that the author has certain convictions and that she hopes this book will effect some changes in child-handling. Child psychotherapists will hold many of these same convictions. For instance, Dr. Leach contradicts the still common confusion between need and greed, and tries to obviate parental fears of ‘spoiling’ by using research results to show that, “All babies demand, but the babies whose needs are met or anticipated do not demand more than the others, they demand less … a baby wants only what he needs”. It is clear that the author also feels that mothers’ interests in their babies’ language and social development should receive as much attention from professionals as do the mothers’ reports of feeding, sleeping and toileting. The emphasis of this book is, therefore, much less exclusively upon the basic physiological processes than is often the case. Moreover, there has been some concern not to produce something which can be used as a handbook of milestones. Emphasis is laid upon the various sequences of development and parents are cautioned that the infant's present development and their expectations as to the immediate future are meaningful only in the light of the past.

responseSet.title: Thoughts on the Maternal Role in in Contemporary Society
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Thoughts on the Maternal Role in in Contemporary Society

Isabel Menzies

Isabel Menzies

Isabel Menzies  

Introduction

This paper focusses attention on society's relationship with death and considers how this affects the role and functions of the mother, particularly in the care of the baby and very young child.

Society's Relationship with Death

Freud's agony and disillusion arising from the First World War led to his perspicacious comments in Thoughts for the Times on War and Death (1915), perspicacious and also, unfortunately, predictive for the future. He comments on our defensiveness against realising the inevitability of our own death or that of people close to us, and adds that this defensive attitude to death “has a powerful effect on our lives. Life is impoverished, it loses in interest, when the highest stake in the game of living, life itself, may not be risked”. The paper returns many times to this point, i.e. that an inadequate relationship with death diminishes the quality of life.

Matters have become no better since, with the Second World War and the development of destructive weapons that beggar the imagination. Many psychoanalysts and other writers have commented on society's difficulty in confronting the meaning of death. Gorer in Death, Grief and Mourning (1965), describes death as a taboo subject, having largely replaced sexuality as such. Mention of death is sometimes treated as an obscenity. Such attitudes inhibit the process of mourning as described, for example, by Freud (1917), Abraham (1924) and Melanie Klein (1940) as do the relative lack in contemporary society of public mourning rituals and private support from friends and relatives. Gorer like Freud comments on the danger of inadequate mourning, stating that it prolongs the symptomatology of mourning, may prevent ultimate recovery and impoverishes the life of the survivors. This impoverishment is increased by the practice of institutionalising the dying, institutionalisation being one of the society's defences against confrontation with intolerable problems. Thus, dying is often not an experience that the dying person shares with close relatives and friends, which makes effective mourning more difficult for them.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Some Notes on Maternal Containment in ‘Good Enough’ Mothering

Martha Harris

Martha Harris

Martha Harris  

In this paper I shall first of all- refer to those theories which I have found most useful in thinking about the many details to be observed in the close study of the early weeks of an infant's interaction with his mother. They are theories which help to bring together configurations seen in the infant observation situation (Bick 1962), with transference phenomena in analytic work with children and adults, in a way that enriches the understanding of both.

I shall then present some sequences from observations of two babies in favourable family circumstances during, those early weeks, following them with excerpts from the beginning of the analysis of a young mother referred for treatment because of acute anxieties during pregnancy and severe depression following the birth of the baby.

The theories are concerned with the prerequisite for mental growth of a primary maternal object who can be an adequate container for the infant's personality, the ‘good enough mother’ about whom Winnicott has written (1965). Detailed study of interaction between individual mothers and infants may help us to formulate better the quality that underlies this quantative differentiation; the constituents that make for that ‘good enough’; and lead to a more convincing recognition of the uniqueness of each relationship, and perhaps the importance of ‘fit’ between the temperament of the mother and the constitution of the baby.

When Freud discovered the phenomenon of narcissism in 1914 his idea was that it was a development from auto-erotism towards object-relations in which the child took his own body as object, in so far as it was identified with, and was indistinguishable from the body of the parent. He considered that this development was an automatic process and called it primary narcissism.

Melanie Klein came to the view that narcissistic identification was brought about by a mental mechanism and was not an automatic process. Eventually in 1946 she described this mechanism implemented by the omnipotent phantasy which she named projective identification. In this phantasy the infant splits off temporarily undesired parts of himself into the object. Excessive use of this mechanism she believed to lead to pathological development including impoverishment of the personality and disturbances in sense of identity.
